## The short version {data-menu-title="The short version"}

::: {.lead}
We can now measure something about this service that nobody has been able to measure before.
:::

::: {.nonincremental}
- Odisha's grievance system holds **1.4 million complaints**
- Its reports count **filings** and **disposals**. Nothing counts **time**, and nothing counts **problems**
- Reading the record properly says cases are routed in a way that costs **11 to 23 days each**
:::

We are not asking you to adopt a model today. We are asking for four things that
would let anyone prove or disprove that number.

::: notes
~90 sec. Set the frame before any detail. Three beats.

One: this is a measurement talk, not a technology talk. The interesting thing we
found is not that a model works, it is that a question nobody could answer turns
out to be answerable.

Two: name the gap immediately, because it is the thing the room will not have
considered. They know their disposal percentage. Ask them, lightly, what the
median age of a pending grievance is. Nobody will know, and it is not on any
screen. That silence is the whole talk.

Three: land the 11 to 23 days but do not oversell it. Say the words "and I will
show you exactly why it is not yet a recommendation" in this first minute. It
buys credibility for everything after, and it stops someone quoting the number
in a press note on Tuesday.
:::

# Part I · What the record already says {data-menu-title="Part I"}

Three findings. None of them needs a model.

::: notes
~15 sec. Signpost. Say explicitly: "nothing in this section involves AI at all.
This is arithmetic on records you already have." That framing is what makes the
section land with a sceptical audience, and it is true.
:::

## Nobody can see how long anything takes {data-menu-title="No time metric"}

::: {.lead}
The reporting screens carry no median age, no time to resolve, no ageing at all.
:::

Disposal percentage and pendency. Both are counts. [measured]{.chip .chip-measured}

Whether a petitioner was actually helped **is** recorded in the database, and no
report uses it. [measured]{.chip .chip-measured}

::: {.visual}
[Visual · the reporting surface, redrawn]{.vtag}
A clean schematic of what the pendency screen shows (counts by office, by status)
beside a greyed-out panel of what it does not show (median age, time to first
action, time to resolve, ageing buckets).
[why]{.why} An absence is hard to see. Showing the present and the absent side by
side makes the gap visible in two seconds, which no sentence does.
[source]{.src} **REDRAWN, NOT SCREENSHOTTED.** The 11 August captures carry real citizen data and are not for circulation. Redraw as a schematic with invented office names.
:::

::: {.src-line}
Verified for the CM Grievance Cell, screens reviewed 11 August 2026. Believed general; a department or Collector login has not been checked.
:::

::: notes
~2 min. This is the most important slide in Part I and possibly in the deck.
Slow down.

The argument: an organisation manages what it reports. This one reports two
counts. So every conversation about performance is a conversation about volume,
and no conversation about speed is even possible, because the number does not
exist. It is not that the number is bad. It is that there is no number.

Land the second bullet hard. The benefit field is *already collected*. Officers
are already ticking it. It reaches the database and then nothing downstream ever
reads it. That is the cheapest possible demonstration that the reporting layer,
not the data layer, is the binding constraint.

Say the scope caveat out loud, do not leave it to the footer. "We verified this
in the CM Grievance Cell. We believe it is the same product everywhere but we
have not logged into a Collector's portal to check, and half an hour of screen
sharing would settle it." Stating the limit of your own evidence before someone
else does is the single highest-return move available in a room like this.
:::

## The disposal rate counts the wrong thing {data-menu-title="Filings, not problems"}

::: {.lead}
Four hundred citizens complaining about one road are four hundred grievances.
:::

The formula on the district report is *resolved ÷ total*, where total is
**filings**. [measured]{.chip .chip-measured}

So the rate rises if an office attracts duplicates and closes them.

::: {.visual}
[Visual · three bars, one district-year]{.vtag}
Filings / distinct problems / distinct citizens, as three descending bars with
the gaps annotated. Existing asset: `docs/value-add-report/figures/fig_dedup.png`
— restyle to the deck palette rather than reusing at report resolution.
[why]{.why} The whole point is the *gap between the bars*. A number cannot show a
gap; three bars show nothing else.
[source]{.src} Demonstration slice, 55,544 redacted records. 37,299 duplicates are the officers' own hand-marked baseline.
:::

::: notes
~90 sec. The road example is the entire slide. Use a real-sounding one: a
stretch of road in one block, four hundred people file about it in a week.

Two consequences, in order of how uncomfortable they are.

First, operational: four hundred filings about one road and two hundred filings
about two hundred unrelated problems look identical in every report you have, and
they need completely opposite responses. One needs a road contractor. The other
needs two hundred separate decisions.

Second, and only say this if the room is receptive: any target set on disposal
percentage is gameable in a direction nobody intended, because the denominator
is filings. This is not an accusation of anyone. It is a property of the formula.

Bridge to the next slide: "and there is a second way the current measures can be
satisfied without anything happening."
:::

---

## Closing a case and solving it are not the same thing {data-menu-title="The closure ladder"}

| Closing wording | Cases | Share | Median days |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Disposed, no action claimed | 472,782 | 39% | **46** |
| Wording outside the standard set | 432,222 | 36% | 25 |
| Disposed with appropriate action | 280,887 | 23% | **54** |
| Disposed, beneficiary benefited | 23,253 | 2% | 44 |

::: {.lead}
Cases closed claiming action took 18 days longer than cases closed claiming none.
:::

[measured]{.chip .chip-measured} over 1,209,144 resolved grievances

::: notes
~2 min. Give the table five seconds of silence, then read only the last column.

The inversion is the point and it is counter-intuitive enough that you should
say it twice. Doing the work takes longer than not doing it. Obvious once said,
and it has a consequence people miss: any objective that rewards speed alone is
maximised by closing everything immediately and doing nothing.

Now the essential caveat, and say it unprompted, because if you do not, someone
in the room will hear an accusation about their officers and stop listening. A
bare disposal is not evidence of a case being mishandled. A question answered, an
ineligible claim correctly refused, and a case quietly dropped all close on the
same phrase. The record cannot tell them apart. That is a limitation of the
record, not a verdict on anyone.

So the finding is not "39% of cases are neglected." The finding is "39% of cases
close on a phrase that cannot distinguish good work from no work, and no
downstream measure notices." That is a *measurement* problem, and it is fixable.

This slide is also the setup for the routing block. Flag it: "hold on to this
table, because it is the reason we could not simply build a system that routes
for speed."
:::

# Part II · What we built {data-menu-title="Part II"}

Six steps, in the order they have to happen.

::: notes
~10 sec. Signpost only. Keep Part II brisk — it is the part the audience expects
and therefore the part that earns least. The routing block is where the talk
actually pays.
:::

---

## The six steps {data-menu-title="Six steps"}

| Step | Today | With this |
|---|---|---|
| Read the petition | Officer reads and retypes | Drafted in ~14 seconds |
| Remove personal detail | Nothing removes it | Stripped before anything else runs |
| Can it be acted on? | Judgement, unrecorded | Flagged with a reason, advisory only |
| Is it a repeat? | Marked by hand when noticed | Same problem counted once |
| Which category? | A dropdown | Ranked; right one in the top three ~9 times in 10 |
| Which office? | ~50 preset routes, no default | Ranked by how fast they actually resolve |

::: {.visual}
[Visual · the pipeline, as one horizontal strip]{.vtag}
Six linked stages left to right, each a simple line icon, with the two that cost
real time (reading the page, drafting the summary) drawn heavier. No stock
robot/AI imagery anywhere.
[why]{.why} The audience needs one picture they can carry out of the room. A
strip they can redraw on a whiteboard is worth more than a detailed architecture
diagram they cannot.
[source]{.src} Self-made schematic, theme-matched. Same visual language as the pipeline figure in the technical report.
:::

::: notes
~2 min. Walk the strip, do not read the table. One sentence per stage, and spend
your time on the two that matter to this audience.

Redaction is first for a reason, and say why: every later step reads what the
citizen wrote, so if personal detail is not removed before matching and grouping,
it is inside all of it. Order is a privacy control, not an implementation detail.

The last row is the one to hold on: this is where the rest of the talk lives.
"Ranked by how fast they actually resolve" is a claim nobody has been able to
make before, and Part III is entirely about what it took to be allowed to make
it.

Do not read out model accuracy figures here. If asked, the honest answer is in
the report and the short version is: these are developmental numbers, measured
against labels no officer has confirmed, and confirming them is the first of the
four asks.
:::

## Fourteen seconds {data-menu-title="Speed"}

::: {.bignum}
14 s
:::
::: {.bignum-sub}
to read a scanned petition and draft a complaint from it · under 1 s for typed text
:::

Officers describe **10 to 15 minutes** to do it by hand. [open]{.chip .chip-open}
*Their estimate, not our observation.*

::: {.visual}
[Visual · stage waterfall]{.vtag}
Horizontal stacked bar of the scanned path, 13.7 s total, segmented by stage.
Reading the page (6.0 s) and drafting the summary (6.6 s) are 92% of it; the five
stages between them total under one second and should be visibly hairline.
[why]{.why} It answers "what would you even optimise?" before anyone asks, and it
quietly shows that all the privacy and triage logic is free.
[source]{.src} `pipeline_latency_development` in the benchmark bundle. n=20 scanned, n=40 typed, synthetic filings, one laptop, sequential.
:::

::: notes
~2 min, and the second half matters more than the first.

Give the 14 seconds, then immediately take it away. Machine seconds are not
officer minutes. The officer still has to read the draft, check it and correct
it. Nothing here has measured whether checking a draft is faster than writing
one from scratch, and a poor draft is *slower* than no draft.

So the honest claim is: this changes what the officer does in those minutes, from
producing to checking. Whether that is quicker is exactly what the pilot would
find out, and it is the second of the four asks.

Being this careful in public is a deliberate move. It is also the reason the 11
to 23 days later in the deck will be believed.

One correction worth making while the subject is open, because it is in our own
earlier material: handwritten Odia is not the bottleneck. Officers fluent in Odia
told us reading the document is not what takes the time, and the ten to fifteen
minutes is the same in either language. The constraint is comprehension and
typing.
:::

## Privacy is the first step, not a review stage {data-menu-title="Redaction"}

Across every redacted complaint in one district-year — **55,544 records** — no
mobile number, Aadhaar number, PAN or non-government email survived.
[measured]{.chip .chip-measured}

Names are harder. On a small hand-corrected set we found **78%** of the personal
details a human marked, and we have not measured how often we remove **too much**.
[open]{.chip .chip-open}

::: {.visual}
[Visual · before / after on one synthetic petition]{.vtag}
Two panels of the same short complaint, identical layout, redactions highlighted
in the accent. Show one *over*-redaction and label it, alongside the correct ones.
[why]{.why} Showing a failure case on your own slide is the most persuasive thing
available, and over-redaction is a real cost: it removes what the officer needs.
[source]{.src} **SYNTHETIC TEXT ONLY.** Write the sample petition by hand for this slide. Never a real complaint, redacted or otherwise.
:::

::: notes
~90 sec. Lead with the strong claim and qualify it honestly.

The strong claim: shaped identifiers — phone, Aadhaar, PAN, email — do not
survive. We checked every record in a district-year, not a sample. That is a
weaker *kind* of claim than an accuracy score, because it only checks the shapes
we know how to look for, and it holds at a scale an accuracy score never could.

The weak claim: names. 78% against a hand-corrected set of 89 pages, and no
precision figure at all, because the set cannot tell an over-redaction from a
name the labeller missed. Say plainly that over-redaction has its own cost.

If someone asks "so is citizen data safe?", the honest answer is: safe from the
identifier types that matter most and that we can verify at scale; not yet proven
on names; and the analysis pipeline never sees unredacted text either way.
:::

The question nobody has been able to ask.

## Every grievance is routed. Nothing says whether the route was right {data-menu-title="Routing today"}

A flat list of about **50 preset routes**. No default. Nothing to indicate which
is better. [measured]{.chip .chip-measured}

::: {.lead}
The only available standard has been: the same as last time.
:::

::: {.visual}
[Visual · the routing chain]{.vtag}
Two example chains drawn as connected nodes — a two-link (Collector → BDO) and a
four-link (CM Cell → Collector → BDO → Collector) — with elapsed days on each
hop and the return leg visibly doubling back.
[why]{.why} Most of the audience has never seen a grievance's path drawn. The
doubling-back leg produces an audible reaction and makes the cost of a handoff
concrete without any statistics.
[source]{.src} Flow census over 1,344,908 decoded chains. Use representative chains, not a real case.
:::

::: notes
~2 min. Describe the officer's actual experience: a dropdown, roughly fifty
entries, unsearchable, in no useful order, no default. Every case, every day.

Then the deeper problem, which is the one that matters. Suppose we build a model
to help with that dropdown. What do we train it on? The only label available is
where cases like this one *went before*. So the very best such a model can do is
reproduce current practice perfectly, including every bad habit in it.

Make it concrete and slightly provocative: a department that receives every land
dispute in a district and resolves none of them is, by that standard, exactly the
right destination. Agreement with history cannot rise above history.

That is why we are not going to show you an accuracy number for route
suggestions. It would be measuring the wrong thing.
:::

## So we changed the question {data-menu-title="The new question"}

::: {.cols}
::: {}
**Old question**

*Where do cases like this one usually go?*

Answerable. Learnable. Ceiling: current practice.
:::

::: {}
**New question**

*Which route actually resolves them fastest?*

Answerable from the same records. Nobody had asked it.
:::
:::

::: {.visual}
[Visual · past practice vs best practice]{.vtag}
The same case fanning out to several candidate routes, each annotated with its
historical resolution time; the historically-chosen one highlighted and visibly
not the quickest.
[why]{.why} This is the conceptual pivot of the whole deck. It should get the one
genuinely designed figure, and the audience should be able to point at it and say
"so you'd have sent it there instead."
[source]{.src} Self-made schematic. Illustrative routes, real orders of magnitude.
:::

::: notes
~2 min. This is the sentence the talk exists to deliver. Slow right down.

Frame it as what it is: not a better model of the same thing, but a different
question about the same records. The data to answer it has been sitting in the
system since 2021. Every grievance carries where it went and how long it then
took. Nobody joined those two facts up and asked which routes work.

Then set expectations for the next four slides honestly: "answering it properly
took four corrections, and I am going to show you all four, because they are the
reason you should believe the number and also the reason I am not going to
recommend acting on it yet."
:::

## The trap {data-menu-title="The trap"}

::: {.lead}
Route for speed alone and you will find the offices that close cases, not the offices that solve them.
:::

Remember: closures claiming action are **18 days slower**. [measured]{.chip .chip-measured}

So the objective has to be constrained — faster, **and** action still taken at
least as often as now.

::: {.visual}
[Visual · the two objectives, side by side]{.vtag}
Left: unconstrained speed, ending in a route that closes everything on day one.
Right: constrained, with the correctness floor drawn as a horizontal line the
policy must stay above.
[why]{.why} It shows we anticipated the obvious failure mode. An audience that
has watched targets get gamed before will recognise this immediately and it buys
enormous credibility.
[source]{.src} Self-made schematic. The floor line reappears numerically on the "honest gap" slide — keep the visual grammar identical.
:::

::: notes
~90 sec. Call back to the closure table explicitly; it is why you showed it.

The argument in one line: if we had optimised for speed alone, we would have
built something that learns to find the offices that dispose of things, and we
would have shipped it with a chart showing a large improvement.

That is worth saying out loud in a government room. It is the exact failure mode
of most performance-management systems, and naming it before you present your own
number is what separates this from a vendor pitch.

So the estimate on the next slides is of a *constrained* policy: it has to be
faster and it has to keep the rate of real action where it is. That constraint is
also where the open question lives.
:::

---

## Four corrections {data-menu-title="Four corrections"}

| Problem | Left uncorrected |
|---|---|
| Recent cases have not had time to close | A busy route looks fast |
| Harder cases get escalated further | Long chains look slow for the wrong reason |
| We picked the best-looking of many routes | The winner looks better than it is |
| Comparing only cases that came out well | Rewards a route for abandoning hard cases |

::: {.visual}
[Visual · waterfall of the estimate]{.vtag}
The naive route-time gap on the left, then a descending waterfall as each of the
four corrections is applied, landing on the final range. Annotate the largest
drop.
[why]{.why} This is the single most persuasive figure available to us. It shows
the number getting *smaller* as the work gets more careful, which is the opposite
of what an audience expects from people presenting their own result.
[source]{.src} Routing-outcome estimator. Ablation and correction steps are in `docs/experiments/routing-outcome-model.tex` §7.
:::

::: notes
~2.5 min. Do not explain the statistics. Explain each correction as a way of
being fooled, in plain words.

One: censoring. A case filed last month has not had time to finish. Count only
finished cases and any route that has been busy recently looks quick.

Two: selection. Harder cases get escalated further, so longer chains carry harder
cases. Some of the extra time is the case, not the chain.

Three: the winner's curse. Compare fifty routes, pick the best-looking, and you
have partly picked noise. We split the data so that the route is chosen on one
part and scored on another.

Four is the subtle one and it is worth the time. If you only compare cases that
came out well, you compare a *different set of cases* under each routing choice.
A route that abandons its hard cases looks excellent. We measured this: making
that mistake makes routing look predictive of duration when it is not, correcting
it removes the effect entirely, and putting the mistake back makes it look larger
than before.

Then the punchline for the waterfall: the number got smaller every time we made
the analysis more careful. That is what should happen. If a number only ever grew
as we checked it, you should not trust it.
:::

## What we found {data-menu-title="The result"}

::: {.bignum}
11–23 days
:::
::: {.bignum-sub}
lost per case to routing, on 454,232 grievances from 2024 [estimated]{.chip .chip-estimated}
:::

Sending each case to the route that has historically resolved that kind of case
quickest, instead of the route it historically went to.

::: {.visual}
[Visual · the interval, not the point]{.vtag}
A single horizontal interval on a day axis, spanning both estimators, with the
historical average marked. Deliberately no bar chart and no single point estimate.
[why]{.why} The width is the message. A point estimate would be quoted out of
context by Wednesday; an interval drawn as an interval is much harder to
misreport.
[source]{.src} Validation cohort 2024, n=454,232. Two estimators; both shown.
:::

::: notes
~90 sec. Deliver the number, then immediately do two things.

Explain what it is: not a saving we achieved, a gap we measured between how cases
are routed and how they could be routed, using only routes that are already in
use for cases like that one. Nothing here proposes a new office or a new process.

Explain the width: two standard methods, and they do not agree closely. We are
showing you both. If we showed you one number it would be because we picked the
one we liked.

Then hand straight over to the next slide: "and there is one more thing I have to
tell you before anyone writes this down."
:::

## The honest gap {data-menu-title="The open question"}

::: {.lead}
Does the faster routing still get action taken? We do not know.
:::

Two standard tests of the same constraint. [open]{.chip .chip-open}

::: {.nonincremental}
- One says it holds comfortably
- The other says it fails
:::

We are not going to report only the one we prefer.

::: {.visual}
[Visual · the constraint, with both answers]{.vtag}
The correctness floor as a horizontal line, with both estimates plotted against
it — one clearly above, one clearly below. Same visual grammar as the "trap"
slide so the audience recognises the line.
[why]{.why} Showing a disagreement you have not resolved, drawn as clearly as a
result, is the most credible slide in the deck. It also makes the fourth ask
self-evidently worth granting.
[source]{.src} Historical rate 0.3868; the two estimates are 0.3530 and 0.4335.
:::

::: notes
~2 min. This slide is why the room should believe the previous one. Present it
with exactly the same energy as the result, not apologetically.

What the disagreement means in plain terms: we can say cases could move faster.
We cannot yet say that moving them faster keeps the same amount of real work
happening. Given the closure table, that is not a hypothetical worry.

Then name the fix, because a problem with a price attached is a decision rather
than a doubt: the reason the two methods disagree is that we are inferring
"was real action taken" from the wording of a closing dropdown. About three
hundred closed cases, read and classified by an officer, would replace the
inference with a fact and settle it. That is roughly two days of one officer's
time, and it is the fourth ask.

If you get one question from this deck, it will be here. The likely one is "so
which number do you believe?" The answer is: we believe the gap is real and we do
not yet believe any recommendation about acting on it, and that is precisely the
distinction we are asking for help to close.
:::

## Officer workload {data-menu-title="Officer workload"}

::: {.bignum}
201,000–302,000
:::
::: {.bignum-sub}
officer-hours spent registering the 1.2M grievances already resolved [estimated]{.chip .chip-estimated}
:::

That is the size of the pot. **We are not claiming to save any of it.**

Three things would reduce it, in ascending order of certainty: drafting instead
of typing; handling a repeat once instead of four times; one assignment decision
instead of three.

::: {.visual}
[Visual · where the hours are]{.vtag}
A simple mass diagram of the total registration hours, with the three mechanisms
sized by how confident we are rather than how large they might be. Confidence as
opacity; magnitude as area.
[why]{.why} Encoding *certainty* visually, not just size, is unusual and it is
exactly the honest thing here — the biggest mechanism is the least certain.
[source]{.src} 1,209,144 resolved × the officers' own 10–15 minute estimate. Arithmetic on a self-reported figure, not a measurement.
:::

::: notes
~90 sec. Be very careful with this number and say why you are being careful.

It is arithmetic on an estimate officers gave us. It is the *denominator*, not a
saving. We put it up because it is the reason the question is worth instrumenting
at all, and because any future claim of time saved has to be stated against
something.

The ordering matters and it is counter-intuitive. The largest possible effect —
checking a draft instead of writing one — is the one we are least sure of,
because a bad draft is slower than no draft. The smallest — not doing the same
repeat complaint four times — is the one we are most sure of, because officers
already recognise that work as waste and mark it by hand.

Do not let anyone leave with "AI saves 300,000 hours." Say the sentence "we are
not claiming to save any of it" out loud.
:::

## What a citizen would notice {data-menu-title="Citizen experience"}

**Shorter waits**, if the routing result holds. [open]{.chip .chip-open}

**Fewer occasions to file the same complaint twice** — a repeat is currently
indistinguishable from a new problem, so the system cannot see its own failures.
[open]{.chip .chip-open}

::: {.lead}
And one warning: the benefit flag is not satisfaction.
:::

Cases closed claiming **no** action carry that flag *more* often than cases closed
claiming appropriate action. [measured]{.chip .chip-measured}

::: notes
~90 sec. The warning is the substance of this slide, so do not rush to it.

There is a field in the database recording whether the petitioner benefited. It
is enormously tempting to report it as a satisfaction measure, and it is the
obvious thing a dashboard project would do. It should not be done, and here is
the evidence: it runs backwards. Cases closed claiming no action carry the flag
more often than cases closed claiming appropriate action. Whatever it is
recording, it is not what its name suggests.

Satisfaction is something a citizen tells you. Nothing in this system currently
asks them. If satisfaction is a goal, a survey channel has to be approved, and
that is a decision rather than an engineering task.

This is a good moment to be quietly ambitious: the system currently cannot see
its own failures, because a citizen who files again because nothing happened
looks exactly like a new complaint. Counting problems instead of filings is what
makes that visible.
:::

---

## Almost everything worth knowing is nearly measurable {data-menu-title="Measurability"}

| What we would want to know | Can we measure it? |
|---|---|
| Citizens wait less | **Yes**, from existing records, once the routing check is settled |
| Fewer repeat complaints | Almost — needs safe citizen-to-problem linkage |
| Cases reach the right office first time | Needs the suggestion-and-override log |
| Action starts sooner | Needs ~300 closing remarks read by hand |
| Officers spend less time per case | Needs timing in the screen, and a staffing figure |
| Citizens are more satisfied | **No** — nothing asks them |

::: {.lead}
What blocks these is instrumentation and permission, not software.
:::

::: notes
~90 sec. This table is the argument of the whole deck compressed into one place,
so give the room time to read it before you speak.

The pattern: read down the right-hand column. Almost every row is blocked on
something small and administrative — a log line, three hundred cases read, a
timer in a screen — and not one row is blocked on a model that does not exist.
The software is the part that is nearly done.

That reframes what we are asking for. Not budget, not procurement, not a
technology decision. Permission to record what is already happening.

Bridge: "which brings me to the four things we are actually asking for."
:::

---

## What we are asking for {data-menu-title="The ask"}

| Decision | What it involves |
|---|---|
| **Let officers check our work** | A few officers review a fixed set of cases we have already scored |
| **Name one department for a trial** | A bounded rollout with a comparison group |
| **Log what is suggested and what the officer does** | One entry when a suggestion is shown, one when it is overridden |
| **Have ~300 closed cases read by hand** | Settles the open routing question. About two days of one officer's time |

::: {.lead}
None of these is a decision about automation.
:::

::: notes
~2 min. This is the slide the meeting is for. Do not hurry it and do not add
anything to it.

Take them in order and give each one its reason in a single sentence.

One: nothing we have shown has been confirmed by an officer. Until it is, we
cannot responsibly recommend anything for real use, and we are not going to.

Two: the effects on officer time and on citizens genuinely cannot be worked out
from historical records. They have to be observed. That is what a bounded trial
with a comparison group is for.

Three is the cheapest and unlocks the most, so give it the emphasis. There is
already a suggestion on the assignment screen today, labelled as AI-suggested.
Nobody knows whether it is any good, because nothing records what officers do
with it. We are not asking to add a model. We are asking to measure the one that
is already there.

Four: three hundred cases, roughly two days, and the open question on the routing
result closes.

End on the line about automation, and mean it: the flag never blocks a filing,
the category never assigns itself, the route is a suggestion. Every one of these
asks is about being able to tell whether any of it is working.
:::

---

## What we are not claiming {data-menu-title="Not claimed"}

::: {.nonincremental}
- No officer minutes saved
- No faster resolution
- No improvement in citizen satisfaction
- No accuracy figure confirmed by an officer
:::

::: {.lead}
Everything here was measured on historical records, or on test filings on a laptop. None of it was measured in a live office.
:::

That is what the second ask would change.

::: notes
~60 sec. Close on the limits, deliberately. It is unusual and it is the right
note to end on with this audience.

The point is not modesty. It is that the difference between "not measured" and
"measured and found to be zero" is the entire value of a pilot, and a room that
understands that difference will grant one.

Then stop talking. Do not add a summary slide. The last thing on the screen
should be what we cannot yet say.

Likely questions and short answers:

*"When could this be live?"* Parts of it run today on a laptop. Live in an office
is a decision about the trial, not about readiness.

*"What does it cost?"* The four asks cost officer time, not money: a review
session, a department, a log line, two days of reading.

*"Can we quote the 11 to 23 days?"* Not as a saving. As a measured gap with an
open question attached, and the sentence about the constraint has to travel with
it.

*"Is the citizen data safe?"* Redaction runs before anything else. Shaped
identifiers verified absent across a district-year. Names not yet proven either
way.
:::
